title: Why Does a Cold Can Sweat? #science #physics
description:
The water on a cold can comes from the air, not from inside. On a hot, humid day (32 °C, 75% humidity) a cubic metre of air carries about 25 g of water vapour. The air touching the can cools to nearly fridge temperature, and at about 4 °C no more than about 6 g per cubic metre can stay as vapour. The rest condenses on the can, like morning dew.

More on water molecules: Why microwaves don't heat food from the inside https://youtu.be/ri17BZl0Iq8

Sources
- Alduchov & Eskridge (1996), Improved Magnus form approximation of saturation vapor pressure, J. Appl. Meteorol. 35: 601–609 (numbers computed for 32 °C at 75% humidity, and 4 °C)
- OpenStax, College Physics 2e, 13.6 Humidity, Evaporation, and Boiling (saturation vapour density table)
- NOAA National Weather Service, Dew point

Next time your glass sweats, you'll know where the water came from. What else "sweats" around you?
